title: Ku hadashay dhibaatada / Talking about past experiences
bridge: In Somali, talking about past experiences often involves using the past tense of verbs, which is formed differently than in English. Unlike English, Somali does not use auxiliary verbs like 'did' for past tense questions or negatives. Instead, the verb itself changes to indicate past tense. Be careful not to directly translate English structures, as Somali relies more on verb conjugation than auxiliary verbs for past tense.
rule: To talk about past experiences in Somali, use the past tense form of the verb. The past tense is typically formed by adding suffixes to the verb stem, such as '-ay' for 'I' and '-ey' for 'you'. For example, 'u dhahay' (I said) and 'u dhehey' (you said). Negatives are formed by adding 'ma' before the verb, e.g., 'ma u dhahay' (I did not say). Questions follow the same structure but with a rising intonation.

common_error.wrong: I did go to the market yesterday.
common_error.correct: Aan u tagey suuqa malintii dabeecad ah.
common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'did' into Somali, but Somali does not use an auxiliary verb for past tense. Instead, the verb itself is conjugated to indicate the past, e.g., 'u tageeyey' (I went).

title: Sameeynta iyo Qorsheynta / Making Plans and Arrangements
bridge: In Somali, making plans often involves a more direct approach compared to English. While English speakers might use indirect questions like 'Would you like to...?', Somali speakers typically use straightforward statements or questions. Additionally, Somali culture values politeness and respect, so expressions of gratitude and courtesy are common. Be cautious not to overuse English phrasal verbs like 'hang out' or 'catch up', as Somali has more literal equivalents.
rule: To make plans in Somali, use the present tense with the verb 'sameeyo' (to do) or 'tagno' (to go) followed by the location or activity. For suggestions, use 'maxaa aad u rabto inaan...' (what do you think if we...). To propose a time, use 'malaa' (tomorrow), 'dabeecad' (evening), or specific times like 'saddex iyo 토토토' (three o'clock). Always end with a polite expression like 'waad ku mahadsantahay' (thank you) or 'hadii la doonayo' (if you want).

title: Fiiri iyo tashriif / Giving Advice and Recommendations
bridge: In Somali, giving advice often involves using the verb 'fiiri' (to think) or 'tashriif' (recommendation), which is more direct than English. Unlike English, Somali advice structures frequently omit subjects, relying on context. Be cautious with word order: Somali is SOV (Subject-Object-Verb), which can feel awkward for English speakers used to SVO.
rule: To give advice in Somali, use the structure '[Verb root] + -aan' for suggestions (e.g., 'fiiraan' = you should think). For stronger recommendations, use 'waxaad u baahan tahay' (you need to). Questions for advice use 'sidee...ba?' (how...?). Remember, Somali often drops pronouns, so 'fiiraan' can mean 'you should think' or 'he/she should think' depending on context.

title: Waxaan u maleynayaa / Expressing Opinions
bridge: In Somali, expressing opinions often involves the verb 'maleynayaa' (to think) or 'u maleynayaa' (I think). Unlike English, where 'I think' can be placed at the beginning or middle of a sentence, in Somali, it typically comes at the beginning for emphasis. Additionally, Somali speakers frequently use 'waxaan' (I) explicitly, whereas in English, the subject 'I' is often omitted in casual speech. Be cautious not to directly translate 'I believe' as it may sound overly formal in Somali.
rule: To express opinions in Somali, use 'Waxaan u maleynayaa' (I think) followed by the opinion. The structure is: 'Waxaan u maleynayaa + sentence'. For negative opinions, add 'ma' before the verb. Example: 'Waxaan u maleynayaa in...' (I think that...). Note that Somali often omits the conjunction 'that' unlike English, where it is commonly used after 'think'.

title: U talin ayax / Agreeing and Disagreeing
bridge: In Somali, agreeing and disagreeing often involve specific phrases and intonation patterns that differ from English. For example, Somali speakers frequently use expressions like 'haa' (yes) and 'maya' (no) but also rely on more nuanced phrases like 'waa inaan talinayo' (I don't agree). Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'I agree with you' as they may sound unnatural in Somali. Additionally, Somali culture values politeness, so disagreements are often softened with phrases like 'maahee' (but) to avoid direct confrontation.
rule: To agree in Somali, use 'haa' (yes) or phrases like 'waa ii talo' (I agree). For disagreement, use 'maya' (no) or 'waa inaan talinayo' (I don't agree). To soften disagreements, use 'maahee' (but) followed by your opinion. Note that Somali often uses verb conjugations to express agreement or disagreement, such as 'u talinayaa' (he/she agrees) or 'uma talinayn' (they don't agree).

common_error.explanation: Directly translating 'I agree with you' into Somali can sound unnatural. Instead, use 'Waxaan ku talinayaa' or the simpler 'Haa, waa ii talo' to express agreement more naturally in Somali.

title: Rutinkaadaada maalin kasta / Daily Routines
bridge: In Somali, daily routines are often described using the present tense, similar to English. However, Somali uses a more explicit structure with the verb 'noqon' (to be) followed by the preposition 'ee' to indicate the time of day, which is different from English's reliance on adverbial phrases. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'in the morning' as they require specific Somali constructions.
rule: To describe daily routines in Somali, use the structure: 'Subax/Galab/Habeen ee [time] waan [verb]'. For example, 'Subax ee eray waan qaataa' (I get up in the morning). The verb 'noqon' is often implied and not explicitly stated. Note that Somali uses 24-hour time, so '7:00' is 'todoba fur' (seven hours).

title: Kula hadal foor iyo caloosha / Talking about health and symptoms
bridge: In Somali, discussing health and symptoms often involves more direct and specific vocabulary compared to English. For instance, Somali uses distinct words for different types of pain (e.g., 'dhan' for general pain, 'dhiig' for headache), whereas English often relies on adjectives like 'bad' or 'severe'. Additionally, Somali speakers tend to use more descriptive phrases to express how they feel, which can be more literal than English idiomatic expressions. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases like 'I have a headache' into Somali, as the structure and word choice differ.
rule: To talk about health and symptoms in Somali, use the verb 'la' (to have) followed by the symptom or condition. For example, 'Waxaan lahayd dhiig' means 'I had a headache.' When describing symptoms, use adjectives like 'adag' (severe) or 'yar' (mild) to specify intensity. For body parts, use possessive pronouns (e.g., 'gacantaydu' for 'my hand'). Remember that Somali word order is Subject-Object-Verb (SOV), which differs from English's SVO structure. Practice using specific symptom vocabulary and avoid literal translations from English.

common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'headache' into Somali conversations. However, Somali uses the word 'dhiig' for headache, not the English loanword. Always use the correct Somali vocabulary for symptoms to sound natural.

title: Su’aalda iyo bixinta caawimo / Making Requests and Offers
bridge: In Somali, making requests and offers often involves more directness than in English. While English uses phrases like 'Could you...' or 'Would you mind...', Somali typically uses the verb 'please' (fadlan) or simply the verb in a polite tone. Additionally, Somali speakers often use the verb 'bixi' (to give) for offers, which is more straightforward than English phrases like 'Can I help you?' or 'Let me...'. Be cautious not to overuse 'fadlan', as it can sound overly formal in casual settings.
rule: To make a request in Somali, use the verb in the imperative form followed by 'fadlan' for politeness. For offers, use the verb 'bixi' followed by the object. For example, 'Bixi macmiilka' (Give me the pen). Note that Somali does not have a direct equivalent to English phrases like 'Would you mind...', so simplicity is key. Always use the appropriate verb form for the subject, but at the A2 level, focus on common verbs and simple sentences.

common_error.wrong: Can you give me the pen?
common_error.explanation: English speakers often directly translate 'Can you...' into Somali, which can sound unnatural. Somali prefers direct requests or offers using 'fadlan' or 'bixi' without the need for 'Can you...'. Stick to simple verb forms and 'fadlan' for politeness.

title: U dhaqan yahay / Expressing Ability
bridge: In Somali, expressing ability is often done using the verb 'u dhaqan yahay' (to be able to), which is more explicit than the English 'can'. Unlike English, Somali does not use a single auxiliary verb for ability; instead, it relies on this specific phrase. Be cautious not to directly translate 'can' as it may lead to awkward or incorrect sentences in Somali.
rule: To express ability in Somali, use the phrase 'u dhaqan yahay' followed by the infinitive of the verb. For example, 'Anigu u dhaqan yahay ku hadash' (I can speak). The phrase remains the same for all subjects and tenses, unlike English where 'can' changes to 'could' in the past. Negation is formed by adding 'ma' before the verb, e.g., 'Anigu ma u dhaqan yahay ku hadash' (I cannot speak).

title: Waxbarasho dhirta / Talking about the weather
bridge: In Somali, discussing the weather often involves more descriptive and vivid language compared to English. While English uses straightforward terms like 'rainy' or 'sunny,' Somali tends to incorporate more expressive phrases and adjectives. Be cautious not to directly translate English phrases, as Somali expressions can be more poetic and context-dependent.
rule: To talk about the weather in Somali, use the verb 'ba' (to be) followed by descriptive adjectives or phrases. For example, 'Waxaa jira qori' means 'It is cold.' Note that Somali often uses the present tense to describe current weather conditions. Adjectives agree in gender and number with the noun they describe, but since weather is typically gender-neutral, this is less of a concern. Common weather phrases include 'Waxaa jira shun' (It is hot) and 'Waxaa ku raacayaa roob' (It is going to rain).

common_error.wrong: It is raining cats and dogs
common_error.explanation: English idioms like 'It is raining cats and dogs' do not translate directly into Somali. Instead, use descriptive phrases like 'Waxaa ku raacayaa roob badan' (It is raining heavily) to convey the same intensity without literal translation.
